Chronology 7 — Jesus: Birth, Mission, Crucifixion

Here the two texts are simultaneously closest and furthest apart: a remarkable shared portrait of Jesus' person, broken by one head-on historical contradiction.

Striking agreement

BibleQur'an
Virgin birthMatt 1; Luke 1Q 19:16–22; 3:47
Title "Messiah"Yesal-Masih (Q 3:45)
Miracles by God's powerYesQ 3:49; 5:110
Healed/raised the deadYesQ 3:49 ("by God's leave")
Sinless / pureYesQ 19:19 ("a pure boy")
Word/Spirit from GodJohn 1Q 4:171
Honoured virgin motherLuke 1Q 19 (whole sura)
Will return before the endYesIslamic tradition; Q 43:61

No other figure is shared in such high relief. (Note: the clay-bird miracle, Q 3:49/5:110, parallels the apocryphal Infancy Gospel of Thomas — an academic literary observation, recorded neutrally.)

The two head-on collisions

1. Deity and sonship — already adjudicated

The Qur'an explicitly denies Jesus' deity and divine sonship (Q 4:171; 5:72–75; 19:88–93). This is the cap. 05 / cap. 09 seam, not re-litigated here.

2. The crucifixion — a factual contradiction

  • Bible: Jesus was crucified, died, was buried, and rose — the center of the message, in all four Gospels and the earliest creed (1 Cor 15:3–8, datable to within a few years of the events).
  • Qur'an: "they did not kill him nor crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them… God raised him to Himself" (Q 4:157–158). Mainstream Muslim reading: a substitution / it only seemed so.

This is the one place the arbiter's own evidentiary rules (Methodology §1: datable physical/historical evidence outranks later tradition) yield a clear lean — on the narrow historical question only:

  • The crucifixion of Jesus under Pilate is regarded by secular and critical historians (e.g. Ehrman, Crossan, Sanders) as one of the most securely established facts of ancient history — multiply attested, early, and meeting the criterion of embarrassment (a crucified messiah was a scandal no one would invent).
  • The Qur'anic denial appears ~600 years later with no earlier documentary or historical corroboration, and the substitution reading is debated even within Islam (e.g. some Ahmadi and modernist readings).

So, strictly as a past event — "was Jesus crucified?" — the evidence strongly favours the Bible's claim. This is a verdict about the event, not about its salvific meaning, which is a theological question outside the arbiter's remit.

Resurrection — flagged, not scored

The death is near-certain historically. The resurrection is a contested historical-and-theological claim (the "minimal facts" debate, Habermas/Licona vs. critics). The arbiter presents both and forces no verdict on the resurrection itself.

Arbiter verdict — Jesus

Present. Extensive shared Christology of the person (virgin birth, Messiah, miracles, sinlessness, return); flat contradiction on deity and on the crucifixion as event.

Weigh.

  • Strong shared core: the agreed material is large and specific — not vague overlap.
  • Decisive on the event: by the dossier's own neutral evidentiary standard, the historicity of the crucifixion is exceptionally well attested; the denial is late and uncorroborated.
  • Out of remit: the meaning of the death (atonement) and the resurrection as a supernatural claim are not scored.

Judge. This is the one chapter where the neutral historical method produces a clear lean: on the bare factual question "was Jesus crucified?", the evidence favours the Bible and runs against Q 4:157 — explicitly limited to the historical event. On who Jesus is (God or prophet) and what the death achieves (atonement or nothing to atone — the cap. 11 seam), the arbiter rules only that each system is internally coherent and that the truth of those claims is out of scope. The seam now reaches its sharpest point: the Fall created the need, and here the texts split on whether the need was met — and even on whether the event happened at all.
